title: Time, randomness and files
summary: The hidden inputs that make tests flaky: the clock (TimeProvider and FakeTimeProvider, timers included), random numbers (inject Random, test properties), and the file system (a temp folder per test, or an abstraction).

steps.title: The clock is an input: TimeProvider
body: `DateTime.Now` inside a class is an input the test cannot set. Since .NET 8 the platform has one abstraction for time, `System.TimeProvider`, and the real one is `TimeProvider.System`. Take it in the constructor:
public bool IsActive(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => clock.GetUtcNow() < startedAt.AddDays(14);
Tests use **`FakeTimeProvider`** from the `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` package. Time stands still until you move it:
var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
Assert.True(policy.IsActive(started));      // the last tick of the trial

- `Advance(...)` moves time forward and **fires timers** created through the provider (`clock.CreateTimer`, `Task.Delay(delay, clock)`, `PeriodicTimer` with a provider, `CancellationTokenSource(delay, clock)`), so a 30-minute timeout runs in a microsecond.
- `SetUtcNow(...)` jumps to a moment; `SetLocalTimeZone(...)` makes "today" independent of the machine; `AutoAdvanceAmount` moves time on each read.
- Always pick a fixed start in tests. A daylight-saving change, a leap day or month end are worth their own test.

steps.prompt: A test creates `new FakeTimeProvider()` with no start time and checks that an invoice created "now" is not overdue. Why is that a weaker test than one with an explicit start?
options: The default start is a fixed date in the year 2000, which hides the scenario: the reader cannot see which day, month end or time zone the test means
FakeTimeProvider without a start reads the real clock
It throws until SetUtcNow is called
Time does not stand still without a start
steps.explain: Without an argument FakeTimeProvider starts at midnight UTC on 1 January 2000. It is deterministic, but the test's story is hidden. Name the moment that matters ("the last day of March, 23:30 in Europe/Berlin") and edge cases become visible.

steps.title: Randomness and files
body: **Random numbers** are another hidden input. Two good options:
- inject a `Random` (production passes `Random.Shared`, tests pass `new Random(42)`), so a seed reproduces a run;

- test **properties** that hold for every output ("8 characters, never `O` or `0`, no duplicates in 1,000 codes") rather than one exact value. That keeps tests green if the algorithm changes and still catches real bugs.
Never assert that a seeded `Random` gives exact numbers across .NET versions, and never use `Random` for security tokens (that is `RandomNumberGenerator`).
**Files**: the simplest honest test uses a real folder that belongs to this test only, and deletes it afterwards:

When code touches many paths, or you need to simulate errors (a locked file, a full disk), an abstraction such as `TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions` (`IFileSystem` in production, `MockFileSystem` in tests) is the common choice. Never write into the repository folder or a fixed path like `C:\temp`: parallel tests and CI agents collide there.

steps.prompt: Match each hidden input to how a test controls it.
pairs: inject a `Random`; tests use a seed and check properties
a temp folder per test from `Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory`
read it once into options and pass the options in

steps.prompt: Deterministic in a test, or a hidden input that needs controlling?
items: `Guid.NewGuid()` used as an id the test asserts on
steps.explain: Culture is the hidden input people forget: `1234.5.ToString()` is `1.234,5` on a German build agent. Pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` where the format is fixed, and test it.

steps.title: Freeze time with FakeTimeProvider
prompt: The trial policy of a subscription service, compiled beside your tests:
public static readonly TimeSpan Length = TimeSpan.FromDays(14);
public DateTimeOffset EndsAt(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => startedAt + Length;
public bool IsActive(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => clock.GetUtcNow() < EndsAt(startedAt);

Write `public class TrialPolicyTests` with at least **five** tests that use a `FakeTimeProvider` with an explicit start (add `using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;`) and `Advance` to move through the trial. Cover the last moment of the trial, the moment it ends, and the days-left display ("13.5 days left" shows 14; after the end it shows 0).
Five planted bugs, one of which quietly reads the real clock.
starter: static readonly DateTimeOffset Start = new(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
solution: static readonly DateTimeOffset Start = new(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);

target: public static readonly TimeSpan Length = TimeSpan.FromDays(14);
public DateTimeOffset EndsAt(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => startedAt + Length;
public bool IsActive(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => clock.GetUtcNow() < EndsAt(startedAt);

mutants.name: the trial is still active at the exact end
mutants.hint: Advance exactly 14 days and expect IsActive to be false.

mutants.name: the trial lasts 15 days
mutants.hint: Your tests should use the 14 days of the rule, not TrialPolicy.Length, at least once.

mutants.name: days left goes negative after the end

require.message: Creates the FakeTimeProvider with an explicit start

hints: Start the clock at a fixed moment and pass it to `new TrialPolicy(clock)`; then `clock.Advance(...)` before each assertion.

The end needs two tests: `Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(14) - TimeSpan.FromTicks(1))` is still active, `Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(14))` is not. Write the 14 days yourself: a test that uses `TrialPolicy.Length` would follow a wrong length.
Days left: after 12 hours expect 14 (rounded up), after 10 days expect 4, after 20 days expect 0.
steps.explain: Time-based rules break at the edges: the last tick, the exact end, rounding. A fake clock lets you stand on each edge and look. Note the length bug: a test that asserts with the code's own constant (`TrialPolicy.Length`) cannot catch a wrong constant. Expected values come from the specification, not the code.
